summary: The final chapter places Sabbath, sabbatical years, and jubilees within the book's chronology and looks forward to a cleansed land without evil. It then commands rest, prepared food, and worship on the seventh day, permits sanctuary offerings, and attaches death penalties to a wide range of prohibited activities before declaring the account complete.
whyItMatters: The book closes by making ordered sacred time a practical obligation for Israel's whole household and land. Its vision of joyful rest must be read together with the severity of the enforcement it demands.

context.author: In the book's Sinai frame an angel recounts this material to Moses. That narrative speaker is distinct from the historical author, whom this chapter does not identify.
context.audience: Moses receives the account inside the story for Israel and its descendants. The historical work addresses Jewish concerns about covenant, inherited stories, and observance; a specific first community is uncertain.
context.date: The narrative uses a chronology counted from creation within its Sinai revelation frame. The historical work is usually placed in the second century BCE; an exact composition date is not established.
context.setting: The angel's concluding instruction to Moses in the wilderness and at Sinai, looking toward entry into Canaan and future observance there.
context.literaryForm: Chronological conclusion and Sabbath legislation ending with an explicit completion formula.

before.text: Passover and unleavened bread have just been assigned fixed dates and sanctuary practices. The conclusion turns to the weekly Sabbath and the larger cycles of years.

here.text: The chapter brings the calendar of jubilees into the household week, specifying both rest and the punitive limits around it.

after.text: This is the book's conclusion: the last verse declares the account of the division of days complete. Its closing instruction leaves the reader with Sabbath observance rather than another narrated chapter.

outline.heading: Sabbaths, jubilees, and a future cleansed land
outline.note: The speaker situates land-rest and jubilees within the chronology from Adam and the future of Israel.

outline.heading: Household rest and its penalties
outline.note: All household members and animals share the rest, while specific violations incur death.

outline.heading: Joyful rest and permitted sanctuary service
outline.note: Eating, drinking, and satisfaction characterize the day, with sacrificial work permitted.

outline.heading: Further prohibitions and the closing formula
outline.note: Travel, labor, violence, hunting, fasting, and war are prohibited, and the account formally ends.

keyVerses.text: Six days shalt thou labour, but on the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God. In it ye shall do no manner of work, ye and your sons, and your men- servants and your maid-servants, and all your cattle and the sojourner also who is with you.
keyVerses.why: The weekly rest explicitly includes children, servants, livestock, and the resident outsider.

keyVerses.text: For great is the honour which the Lord has given to Israel that they should eat and drink and be satisfied on this festival day, and rest thereon from all labour which belongs to the labour of the children of men save burning frankincense and bringing oblations and sacrifices before the Lord for days and for Sabbaths.
keyVerses.why: The Sabbath is described positively through honor, satisfied eating and drinking, and rest.

keyVerses.text: The man who does any of these things on the Sabbath shall die, so that the children of Israel shall observe the Sabbaths according to the commandments regarding the Sabbaths of the land, as it is written in the tablets, which He gave into my hands that I should write out for thee the laws of the seasons, and the seasons according to the division of their days. Herewith is completed the account of the division of the days.
keyVerses.why: The final verse unites the severe penalty, the written calendar laws, and the declaration that the account is complete.

questions.question: Why end a long ancestral history with Sabbath rules?
questions.answer: The closing speech presents the division of days, years, and jubilees as the framework of the history just recounted. It then turns that framework into recurring observance and explicitly declares the account complete.

questions.question: What is a “jubilee” doing in this chapter?
questions.answer: It is part of the larger reckoning of years and year-weeks, connected here with the land's Sabbaths and the chronology from Adam. The speaker also says some timing concerning the land awaits entry, so not every practical calculation is supplied here.

questions.question: Who must be allowed to rest?
questions.answer: The command includes the addressed Israelites, their children, male and female servants, cattle, and the sojourner with them. It portrays Sabbath as a household-wide cessation of labor rather than a privilege reserved for the household head.

questions.question: What positive activities define the day?
questions.answer: Prepared food allows eating, drinking, satisfaction, and rest, together with blessing God. Calling the day a festival helps explain why the later list includes fasting among prohibited practices.

questions.question: What work is permitted at the sanctuary?
questions.answer: Burning frankincense and bringing offerings and sacrifices are specifically allowed. The text treats that continuing service for Israel as an exception within the general prohibition on labor.

questions.question: How severe are the Sabbath penalties?
questions.answer: The chapter repeatedly demands death and extends it to activities including carrying burdens, drawing unprepared water, sexual intercourse, travel, lighting fire, hunting, fasting, and making war. These are the text's laws and must be stated without turning them into modern enforcement instructions.

questions.question: Does the ban on striking or killing supply a full discussion of emergencies?
questions.answer: No. The list prohibits striking, killing, and war but does not discuss rescue situations or spell out an emergency exception. A guide should acknowledge that limit instead of importing a later legal resolution and presenting it as this chapter's own wording.

questions.question: What does the promised end of evil describe?
questions.answer: The text looks toward a time when Israel is cleansed, dwells securely, and no Satan or evil one remains. That is its future theological hope, not a statement that the present world has already reached those conditions.

glossary.def: The major year cycles used to organize the book’s chronology and linked here with the land’s Sabbath observance.
A resident outsider included with the household in the command to rest.
Offerings permitted at the sanctuary on the Sabbath as part of continuing worship.
The aromatic substance burned in the sanctuary service that the chapter permits on the Sabbath.
